title: Segregation at the Cotton Club
summary: Greer says prices kept most Black patrons away; Bill Robinson was welcome.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Never played with the band. Didyou-- how did the band members feel about the segregated policy at the Cotton Club.

We were so busy -- we didn't pay it no mind. Because in the first place, we had colored people come up there, but the prices were so high. The average colored person back off. They could go to Small's Paradise and them clubs, and that -- when you come in the Cotton Club, you sit down, you're going to spend a lot of money. They didn't care if they were colored. You could come in. But the average guy, a rumor hear about this and that and the other, they'd back off. Cost a lot of money. Of course, them colored guys in the rackets, they associated like working for the guys, they'd come up and sit down and spend money and have a ball.
Yeah, that was what Jimmy Crawford who came in there told me. Told me the only colored people he knew were the racketeers.

They never stopped Bill Robinson, he was a big star. They put the red carpet out for him. But the porter it was too much pressure, ordinary layman out there/ carrying them bricks and working, / he couldn't stand that. It was a regular Broadway production we put on, they could afford that. Stars, from the Ziegfeld show, and madames, all the big madames come up there.
